Precious Metals Quarterly 1Q2007 

# Executive summary 

## Rally resumed 

After a shaky start to 2007, precious metals’ prices moved steadily higher during the first quarter.  Though the sector succumbed to the weak sentiment that swept through the global equity and commodity markets in early March, platinum and palladium have more than recovered their losses, while gold and silver are currently in a gentle up-trend. 

We do not anticipate a repeat performance of last year’s fireworks, but the major precious metals are expected to build on their average 2006 prices.

Precious Metals Quarterly 1Q2007    Executive Summary 

## Gold: fundamentally sound 

2006 was marked by spectacular price movements for gold: the average price for the year was 36% higher than in 2005; the price at the end of December was 24% higher than the price one year earlier, while the year’s high – $725/oz – was 38% higher than the year’s low.  The extent and strength of future investor interest and the extent to which central banks turn purchasers rather than sellers look set to be the key determinants of how far, and for how long, the price rise continues. 

- Import data for India and Turkey, along with market reports, suggest that demand for jewellery and related physical markets was reasonably strong in January.  However indications are that it faded in February as the price rose higher.  Market reports indicate moderate demand in March after the price fall.  From mid-February there has been a dearth of major gold-buying occasions, coupled with a lull in the Indian wedding season but jewellery buyers now appear comfortable with prices in excess of $600/oz, providing solid underpinning to the gold market. 

- From a technical viewpoint, the biggest threat to the continuation of the gold up-trend comes from the contrarian (bear) traders, with gold now becoming an attractive target.  The event most likely to pull these opportunistic shorts into the old market will be a strong (capitulation) rally, which marks the last gasp of the bull-run. 

- Trends in demand and supply

, however, suggest that the bull-run has further to go.  We expect mine output to rise, but the extent of the rise will be limited.  An additional increase will be provided from a reduction in de-hedging.  There is some scope for further reduction but the irreducible minimum must be approaching.  There is some new hedging, primarily associated with the financing of new projects, but sentiment in many companies remains firmly against the practice.  Thus, for the moment it seems unlikely that a major wave of new hedging will add to supply. 

- Signatories to the 2<sup>nd</sup> Central Bank Gold Agreement collectively sold 103 tonnes less than their annual limit during the second year of the Agreement.  They look to sell no more, and probably less, in future years.  Central banks outside of the CBGA are starting to become net buyers, albeit only to a small extent as yet. 

- CRU believes that investor interest in gold will be maintained for the next two to three years; it will remain strong and could intensify.  Exchange Traded Funds will continue to spread to different areas of the world and attract continuing inflows.  We expect some further move of pension and other long-term institutional holders into gold as well as ongoing interest from private and family funds.  This combined with the limited supply will push the price up further. 

- Jewellery demand will be hurt by the rising price, although we expect some temporary recovery in 2007 from 2006 levels on the assumption that the price is less volatile this year than last.

## Platinum: building on $1,100/oz 

Platinum maintained a gentle up-trend from mid-December through to early March, primarily in response to supply-side news.  A sell-off in the global equity and commodities markets saw platinum fall by almost 7% to a low of $1,165/oz on 5 March, but the correction was shortlived.  The price subsequently challenged the $1,250/oz level on the back of a shortage of platinum sponge that was first reported in mid-March.  This shortage remains today (early April), with sponge trading at a premium to Zurich ingot by up to $3/oz.  Rumours regarding the introduction of an exchange-traded fund in platinum again materialised, but while this did provide some support to prices, there was not the stratospheric reaction that we saw last November.  CRU maintains its view that an ETF would be unlikely to receive regulatory approval given the strong opposition it would face. 

- Platinum demand in the autocatalyst sector is forecast to grow by an annual average of 4.6% until 2011.  The underlying global trend for vehicle production is still very positive with Asia leading the way.  Furthermore, the stage is set for the market share of diesel-engine vehicles to increase in the USA and new Federal emission standards for heavy-duty vehicles come into force this year. 

- CRU expects the platinum market to move into surplus by more than 100koz from 20

08, mostly on the back of mine expansions in South Africa, but also through secondary recovery with the increased availability of platinum-bearing spent autocatalysts.  Demand for the metal will continue to grow over the forecast period driven by offtake in the autocatalyst sector, which will offset weakness in the jewellery sector in the short term.  We are forecasting a long-term average platinum price of $1,015/oz. 

## Palladium: investment demand key to maintaining prices 

Palladium broke out of its trading range in a technically significant manner at the end of 2006, finally reaching $340/oz and then $350/oz by the end of January on the back of fresh fund buying and strong gains in platinum.  Like its sister metal, palladium too succumbed to the weakness in the equity markets in early March but from a technical standpoint the weakness in this market was a lot less than had been registered in other PGMs. 

- Despite palladium’s rather poor fundamental outlook, speculators have continued to take up long positions on NYMEX.  It is likely that the conspicuous lack of volatility has had a bearing on investor attitudes towards this metal, being an attractive quality to those looking for a long-term bull strategy.  The market will therefore be vulnerable to changes in sentiment in the future, but with the platinum and gold markets expected to remain strong in the short- to medium-term we do not expect the palladium price to fall off sharply. 

- The market is still reliant on Russian shipments; however there will be less scope for large stock sales in the future and this will help rein in the market surplus over the forecast period. 

- CRU forecasts an average palladium price of $339/oz over the 2007 to 2011 period.

## Silver:  outlook weakens further amid shakier LME metal price movements 

The London Fix for silver remained above $12.21/oz during the first quarter of 2007, a feat that has not been achieved since Q4 1980.  As in the early 1980s, high prices are again doing what economics would suggest – demand is being dampened and supply is being encouraged. 

- Demand remains restrained by high prices.  For the moment, silver’s use in jewellery and silverware is weak, and while prices are high, competing discretionary luxury items are being marketed heavily.  Demand from the imaging sector continues to be eroded.  Silver’s use in electronics and electrical applications continues to grow well, but while the silver industry has been very active in encouraging the development of new uses for silver, these are being hindered by today’s prices.  Global offtake is therefore unlikely to recover to the level reached in 2000 until 2011. 

- Mine supply looks set to increase by over 40% this decade, and is due, on the basis of our forecasts, to lift above ground silver stocks to the equivalent of 1.7 years of consumption by 2011. 

- The market does need extra mine supply.  Above ground stoc

ks were drawn down during the 1990s and early 2000s to reach a level equivalent to not much more than one year of consumption in 2003-2004, having peaked at the equivalent of over five years in the 1980s. Moreover, scrap supplies are being increasingly constrained by the erosion of silver’s use in photography, and thus mine supply must increasingly reflect total global demand. 

- It is not just primary silver mining that is experiencing a renaissance.  Exploration and evaluation of projects for all metals is booming.  The argument that silver’s largely byproduct status makes supply relatively inelastic has merit, however, high zinc, lead, copper and gold prices are also to result in higher silver mine supply. 

- The combination of demand struggling to grow and massive additional mine supply will maintain significant market surpluses during our forecast period.  We continue to expect these to eventually take prices lower, just as extra supplies of other metals will reduce the price of these.  With this in mind, we forecast mine supply growth falling back by 2011. This will moderate the market’s surplus and halt further increases in the stock ratio.  A comfortable, but not excessive, stock position should hold prices around long-run levels. However, a prolonged period of high prices for all metals run the risk of prompting even greater supply growth than we forecast.  This will result in significantly higher stock build.

## CRU’s precious metals service 

We changed the Precious Metals Service, both the Monitor (since the November 2004 issue) and the Quarterly (since the 1Q2005 issue), following the findings of the independent market research we commissioned in 1H2004.  We value any feedback to any of the authors of this report. 

The aim of the changes is to improve the quality of our service, by still providing our overall market outlook for each metal, but in a more concise way than before.  This will leave more scope for more timely and focussed analysis delivery on a continual basis.  In essence, each chapter of the precious metals we cover, i.e. gold, platinum, palladium and silver, includes the following: 

1. **Recent trends** - a summary of latest developments in prices and the key price drivers. 

2. **Storyboard** - a presentation of our outlook in a series of charts.  This encapsulates the factors we feel will shape prices over the forecast period as well as the impact that the price outlook will have on the metal’s fundamentals, whether these are price determining, as is the case for pgms, or price taking, as is the case for gold and silver. 

3. **Forecast Update** – a more detailed look at a particular topic of interest that we feel will have an influence on prices going forward. 

4. **Tables** – historical and forecast data of prices and other key variables to enhance our market view. 

The storyboard and the tables are available as downloads from our extranet site.

## Data sources 

The historical data presented in this report is based on estimates provided by a variety of sources, CPM Group, Johnson Matthey (JM), World Gold Council (WGC), International Financial Statistics (IFS), JD Power, London Bullion Market Association (LBMA), World Bureau of Metal Statistics (WBMS

), GTIS trade statistics, company websites and written reports.  However, CRU’s interpretation of the data may or may not coincide with those expressed in these various sources.  The forecast is exclusively CRU’s outlook.
